title: No. 2 — Concerning Dangers from Foreign Force and Influence (Jay)
paragraphs: When the people of America reflect that they are now called upon to decide a question whose consequences must prove one of the most important ever to engage their attention, the wisdom of taking a comprehensive and serious view of it will be obvious.

Nothing is more certain than the indispensable necessity of government, and it is equally undeniable that whenever and however government is created, the people must give up some of their natural rights in order to vest it with the powers it needs. It is therefore well worth considering whether it would serve the interests of the American people more for them to be, for all general purposes, one nation under one federal government, or to divide themselves into separate confederacies and grant the head of each the same kinds of powers proposed for one national government.

Until recently, it has been an accepted and unchallenged opinion that the prosperity of the American people depended on their continuing firmly united, and the wishes, prayers, and efforts of our best and wisest citizens have been steadily directed to that goal. But politicians have now appeared who insist this opinion is mistaken, and that instead of looking for safety and happiness in union, we ought to seek it by dividing the States into separate confederacies or sovereignties. However extraordinary this new doctrine may seem, it has its advocates—and certain figures who once opposed it strongly are now among them. Whatever arguments or inducements have produced this change in the views and statements of these gentlemen, it would not be wise for the people at large to adopt these new political tenets without being fully convinced that they rest on truth and sound policy.

It has often given me pleasure to observe that independent America was not made up of detached and distant territories, but that one connected, fertile, wide-spreading country was the inheritance of our western sons of liberty. Providence has, in a special way, blessed it with a variety of soils and products and watered it with countless streams for the delight and convenience of its inhabitants. A succession of navigable waters forms a kind of chain around its borders, as if to bind it together, while the noblest rivers in the world, running at convenient distances, give them highways for the easy exchange of friendly aid and the mutual transport and trade of their various commodities.

With equal pleasure I have often noted that Providence has chosen to give this one connected country to one united people—a people descended from the same ancestors, speaking the same language, professing the same religion, attached to the same principles of government, very similar in their manners and customs, who, by their joint counsels, arms, and efforts, fighting side by side throughout a long and bloody war, have nobly established general liberty and independence.

This country and this people seem made for each other, and it appears that Providence intended an inheritance so fitting and convenient for a band of brothers, joined by the strongest ties, never to be split into a number of unsocial, jealous, and alien sovereignties.

Similar sentiments have until now prevailed among all classes and groups of people among us. For all general purposes we have consistently been one people, each individual citizen everywhere enjoying the same national rights, privileges, and protection. As a nation we have made peace and war; as a nation we have defeated our common enemies; as a nation we have formed alliances, made treaties, and entered into various compacts and conventions with foreign states.

A strong sense of the value and blessings of union led the people, very early on, to set up a federal government to preserve and perpetuate it. They formed it almost as soon as they had a political existence—indeed, at a time when their homes were in flames, when many of their citizens were bleeding, and when the progress of war and devastation left little room for the calm and mature inquiry and reflection that must always precede the formation of a wise and well-balanced government for a free people. It is no surprise that a government created in such unfavorable times should, on trial, prove greatly deficient and inadequate to the purpose it was meant to serve.

This intelligent people perceived these defects and regretted them. Still as attached to union as they were enamored of liberty, they observed the danger immediately threatening the former and more remotely threatening the latter. Persuaded that ample security for both could only be found in a national government more wisely framed, they, as with one voice, called the recent convention at Philadelphia to take that important subject under consideration.

This convention was made up of men who possessed the confidence of the people, many of whom had become highly distinguished by their patriotism, virtue, and wisdom in times that tried the minds and hearts of men. They undertook the difficult task. In the mild season of peace, with minds free of other concerns, they spent many months in cool, uninterrupted, daily consultation. Finally, without being intimidated by power or moved by any passions except love for their country, they presented and recommended to the people the plan produced by their joint and very unanimous deliberations.

Admit, as is the fact, that this plan is only RECOMMENDED, not imposed. Yet remember that it is recommended neither for BLIND approval nor for BLIND rejection, but for the calm and candid consideration that the size and importance of the subject demand and ought to receive. But this (as was noted in the previous paper of this series) is more to be wished than expected—that it will actually be considered and examined that way. Past experience teaches us not to be too hopeful in such expectations. It is not yet forgotten that well-grounded fears of imminent danger led the American people to form the memorable Congress of 1774. That body recommended certain measures to its constituents, and events proved their wisdom; yet it is fresh in our memories how soon the press began to teem with pamphlets and weekly papers attacking those very measures. Not only did many government officials, who obeyed personal interest, work tirelessly against them, but so did others—from a mistaken sense of consequences, from undue influence of old loyalties, or from ambition aimed at goals not aligned with the public good. Many were indeed deceived and misled, but the great majority of the people reasoned and decided wisely; and they are happy now to reflect that they did so.

They considered that the Congress was made up of many wise and experienced men. That, gathered from different parts of the country, they brought with them and shared a variety of useful information. That, during the time they spent together inquiring into and discussing the true interests of their country, they must have acquired very accurate knowledge on that score. That they personally had a stake in the public liberty and prosperity, and that it was therefore as much their inclination as their duty to recommend only such measures as they truly thought prudent and advisable, after the most mature deliberation.

These and similar considerations led the people to rely heavily on the judgment and integrity of the Congress, and they took its advice in spite of the various tricks and efforts used to discourage them. But if the people at large had reason to trust the men of that Congress—few of whom had been fully tested or generally known—they have still greater reason now to respect the judgment and advice of the convention. For it is well known that some of the most distinguished members of that earlier Congress, since tested and justly approved for their patriotism and abilities, who have grown old in the gathering of political experience, were also members of this convention and brought into it their accumulated knowledge and experience.

It is worth remarking that not only the first, but every subsequent Congress, as well as the recent convention, has invariably joined with the people in believing that the prosperity of America depended on its Union. To preserve and perpetuate it was the great object of the people in forming that convention, and it is also the great object of the plan the convention has recommended for adoption. With what justification, then, or for what good purpose, are some men at this particular moment trying to belittle the importance of the Union? Or why is it suggested that three or four confederacies would be better than one? I am persuaded in my own mind that the people have always thought rightly on this subject, and that their universal and uniform attachment to the cause of the Union rests on great and weighty reasons, which I will try to develop and explain in some of the papers to follow. Those who promote the idea of substituting a number of separate confederacies for the plan of the convention seem clearly to foresee that rejecting it would put the continuance of the Union in the utmost jeopardy. That would certainly be the case, and I sincerely wish every good citizen could see just as clearly that, whenever the dissolution of the Union arrives, America will have reason to exclaim, in the words of the poet: "FAREWELL! A LONG FAREWELL TO ALL MY GREATNESS."
